summary: This RFC defines a Deprecation HTTP response header field that tells API clients a resource is, or will be, deprecated. It also defines a "deprecation" link relation that can point to documentation about the deprecation. Together they let services warn clients automatically before something goes away.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a sticker on a toy saying "we will stop making this soon." Programs that use a web service can read the sticker and know it is time to switch.

questions: how to signal an api is deprecated in http
how to deprecate an http api endpoint
api lifecycle management with deprecation header
subtitle: Signal to API clients that a resource will or has been deprecated

tldr.problem: When API providers want to retire or replace endpoints, clients have no standard way to receive advance warning. Services send out breaking changes without giving developers time to update their applications.
tldr.mechanism: A new HTTP response header called Deprecation carries a timestamp indicating when the resource was or will be deprecated. An optional Link header with relation type "deprecation" points to documentation explaining the change and migration path.
tldr.outcome: API providers can now warn clients automatically before changes take effect. Developers receive runtime signals to update their code instead of discovering issues through broken requests.

today: RFC 9745 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It is now registered in IANA, and API providers can begin using the Deprecation header in their responses to communicate lifecycle information to clients.

sections.title: Deprecation in HTTP APIs
sections.content:
As HTTP APIs evolve, services need to retire old endpoints, change behavior, or require clients to use different methods. Developers who build applications against these APIs need to know when changes are coming.

Before this RFC, there was no standard way for a server to communicate deprecation. Services might announce it on a blog, send an email, or post a notice on their website. Application developers might not see these announcements, and their applications would break when the old endpoint disappeared.

The Deprecation HTTP header solves this by providing a standard, machine-readable signal that clients can detect at runtime. Combined with documentation links, it allows API providers to inform developers of upcoming changes in real time, giving them a chance to update their code.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites and programs talk to each other using HTTP. This header is like a note the website sends saying "I am going away soon." Programs can read the note and warn the person using them to switch before it is too late.

sections.title: The Deprecation Header Format
sections.content:
The Deprecation header is a simple HTTP response header field. Its value is a single date in the format defined by RFC 9651 (Structured Field Values for HTTP), shown as a timestamp in seconds since the Unix epoch.

Example: Deprecation: @1688169599

This indicates the resource was deprecated on Friday, June 30, 2023 at 23:59:59 UTC. The date may be in the past (the resource was already deprecated) or in the future (the resource will be deprecated on that date).

The date is required. Each resource gets one Deprecation header per response. The header applies specifically to the resource identified in the response, though resource providers may document that increased scope (such as the entire API) also applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is just three words: the word "Deprecation" and a date (like a restaurant saying "closing on June 30"). Programs can understand it without reading a whole paragraph.

sections.title: How Developers Use the Header
sections.content:
When a client application receives a response with the Deprecation header, a developer can configure their application to log a warning, display an alert, or take other actions.

For example, a library or framework might emit a deprecation warning to the developer console whenever a deprecated API endpoint is called. This gives developers immediate feedback during testing and development. Over time, developers can plan their migration path and update their code to use replacement endpoints.

The scope of deprecation can vary. Most commonly, the Deprecation header on a specific resource applies only to that resource. However, an API provider can document that it also applies to related resources (like all endpoints under an API version prefix). Since increased scoping is invisible to clients unaware of the rules, it serves only as a hint, not a guarantee.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program gets the header, it can tell the developer "this thing is going away." The developer then has time to find the new thing and switch to it.

sections.title: Linking to Deprecation Documentation
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new link relation type called deprecation for use with the Link header field (RFC 8288). This allows a server to point clients to documentation about the deprecation.

Example:

Link: <https://developer.example.com/deprecation>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html"

The linked resource typically contains information like: why the resource is deprecated, what resource should be used instead, migration guidance, and the timeline for the deprecation. This documentation can be human-readable (HTML) or machine-readable (JSON Schema, OpenAPI spec, etc.).

A resource provider might publish deprecation documentation even before setting a Deprecation header, as a way of explaining the deprecation policy. This allows developers to understand the policy before the actual deprecation begins.
sections.plainLanguage: The link relation is like a URL on the sign saying "go here for more info." The developer can click the link and read instructions for what to do next.

sections.title: Coordinating Deprecation and Sunset
sections.content:
The RFC builds on another standard called the Sunset header (RFC 8594). The Sunset header indicates when a resource will stop responding entirely. The Deprecation header indicates when the resource becomes deprecated (the hint to migrate).

Example:

Deprecation: @1688169599Sunset: Sun, 30 Jun 2024 23:59:59 UTC

The Deprecation date should always be earlier than or equal to the Sunset date. The Deprecation date gives developers notice and time to migrate. The Sunset date is the deadline when the resource will actually stop working. Developers should consult with the resource provider if these dates seem inconsistent.

Together, these headers provide a complete lifecycle signal: first, the Deprecation header warns that change is coming; then, after the Sunset date arrives, the resource becomes unresponsive or behaves differently, and clients must use the replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: The Deprecation header says "change is coming," and the Sunset header says "it stops working on this date." Developers use the time between them to update their programs.

sections.title: Security and Reliability of Deprecation Signals
sections.content:
The Deprecation header is a hint, not a guarantee. A server MAY send it, and clients SHOULD respond appropriately, but it is optional information. Applications must function correctly even if the server never sends a Deprecation header.

Developers should verify that deprecation information is authentic by checking if it is served over HTTPS and consulting official documentation. If the Link header points to a resource served over HTTP (not HTTPS), the developer should be cautious, as the link content is not integrity-guaranteed.

If the Deprecation date is in the past, the behavior of the resource may have changed, and client applications can no longer assume the resource behaves as it did before the deprecation date. Developers should consult the provider about what changed.

If a misconfiguration creates an inconsistency (such as Sunset before Deprecation), developers SHOULD contact the API provider to clarify. The header alone cannot enforce correctness; correct behavior depends on proper configuration and monitoring by the service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is just a hint, not a lock. The program should still work without it. Be careful about following links unless they are secure, and ask the API owner if something looks wrong.
